summary:
Borno stands under the national framework: Nigeria criminalises same-sex conduct under the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 (SSMPA), which also bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, public shows of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and which Human Rights Watch (October 2016) records police using to justify torture and arbitrary arrests. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026) records same-sex sex between men as criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment, and Sharia law in all twelve northern states criminalising same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions. Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute, but Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public, and whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here.

Borno is one of the twelve northern Nigerian states that had adopted Shari'a into criminal legislation by 2002, according to Human Rights Watch's 2004 report, with Shari'a courts holding criminal jurisdiction over Muslims beyond federal law. The UK Home Office note (June 2025) states that Islamic law applies to Muslims in the twelve northern states and criminalises same-sex sexual acts both between men and between women; the maximum penalty for sodomy for men is death in all twelve states, and penalties for lesbianism range from death to flogging and imprisonment. That note carries a dedicated section on enforcement of Sharia provisions and the attitude of the hisbah, the morality police.

Borno's criminalisation of same-sex conduct rests on Borno legislation as well as the federal framework. The state's own statute on prostitution, homosexuality, brothels and other sexual immoralities (2000) was signed by Governor Kachalla on 10 December 2000 and gazetted in Borno State Gazette No. 42 Vol. 26 on 18 October 2001. Section 3 makes engaging in prostitution, lesbianism, a homosexual act or pimping an offence in the state; section 7 provides that any person who engages in sexual intercourse with another person of the same gender shall upon conviction be punished with death; section 4 deems all brothels closed on commencement; and section 9 assigns jurisdiction to the Upper Sharia Courts, Area Courts and Magistrate Courts.

Borno additionally enacted its own Sharia Penal Code Law 2001, signed into law on 3 March 2003, with no operation date or gazette identified in the sourcebook's list of enacted Sharia Penal Codes. The editor notes that the Borno text was obtained only in May 2006, after the volume's annotation had been completed, which is why Borno is not among the individually annotated codes. The parallel Sharia layer for Borno therefore rests on a Borno-specific enactment rather than on federal or umbrella coverage.

Violence and extortion risk attaches to the national regime. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, the TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found on a highway in Abuja hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing, and the Dial (February 2025) records that six months after the killing no suspects had been charged. TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports that Okafor, a 24-year-old man stopped by Lagos police, was struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay. The Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advice for Nigeria, as reported by Sahara Reporters, warns LGBT+ travellers of attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under Sharia law in northern states.

The only trans-specific imprisonment case in these sources concerns Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), who pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine, served in a maximum-security prison in Lagos and completed on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in, indicating that placement between male and female sections was left to discretion; an October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.
tangentialFactors:
Borno's own statute sets a penalty the federal SSMPA does not: death for same-sex intercourse under section 7, against a maximum of 14 years' imprisonment under the national act. The two layers are cumulative rather than alternative, so a visitor or resident assessed under the federal text alone would understate the maximum exposure in this state.

The evidence base for Borno is documentary rather than judicial. The state statute is reproduced in a scholarly sourcebook and the Sharia Penal Code Law 2001 appears in a list of enactments, but no court decision, charge sheet or arrest record for Borno appears in these sources. The absence of case material is a limit of the inventory, not a finding that the provisions go unenforced.

The sourcebook's annotation gap is itself a caution about the record: the Borno text reached the editor in May 2006, after the volume had been completed, so Borno is missing from the individually annotated codes even though the enactment exists. Comparable states in the same twelve-state group are documented in greater detail, which makes Borno look thinner on the page than the underlying law is.

The hisbah, or morality police, appear in the UK Home Office note as a standing enforcement actor whose attitude toward Sharia provisions is documented in a dedicated section. Their presence distinguishes the twelve Sharia states from the rest of Nigeria, where enforcement runs through federal police alone.

Bobrisky's case is a national correctional-placement precedent rather than a Borno matter, but it bears on any trans person remanded in a Nigerian prison: an October 2024 panel found that maximum-security placement violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act for a first-time offender, while press coverage at sentencing treated the male-or-female section question as an open discretionary decision.
localsOnly:
Residents of Borno face three overlapping layers of criminal law: the federal Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014, the state statute on prostitution, homosexuality, brothels and other sexual immoralities signed in December 2000 and gazetted in October 2001, and the state's Sharia Penal Code Law 2001 signed on 3 March 2003.

Sharia criminal jurisdiction in Borno applies to Muslims and extends beyond federal law, a position Human Rights Watch recorded in 2004 as settled by 2002. Section 9 of the state statute assigns jurisdiction over its offences to the Upper Sharia Courts, Area Courts and Magistrate Courts, so a same-sex conduct charge can be heard in more than one court tier.

Section 4 of the state statute deems all brothels closed on commencement, and section 3 makes pimping an offence alongside lesbianism and homosexual acts. These provisions operate independently of the SSMPA's bans on cohabitation, public displays of a same-sex relationship and gay organisations.

For Muslim women, the exposure recorded in the UK Home Office note covers lesbianism with penalties ranging from death to flogging and imprisonment; for Muslim men, sodomy carries the death penalty as the maximum in all twelve Sharia states, including Borno.

Housing and placement for a trans person in custody is governed by the Nigerian Correctional Service Act, which an October 2024 investigative panel found was breached by maximum-security placement of a first-time offender. The panel dismissed the bribery allegations that had been raised alongside that finding.
outOfScopeNotes:
No trans-specific incident, no hisbah case and no court-level study covering Borno appears in this inventory. Whether the hisbah in Borno have detained or prosecuted anyone under the state statute is unresolved on the sources available here.

The commencement status of Borno's Sharia Penal Code Law 2001 is unresolved: the sourcebook records the signature date of 3 March 2003 but identifies no operation date and no gazette reference, and the editor's note explains that the text arrived after annotation was complete.

Whether the 2022 proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public have been enacted is not settled by these sources, and no Borno-specific provision on gender expression is recorded here.

The frequency and manner of enforcement of Borno's section 7 death penalty are not sourced. No execution, commutation or sentence under that section is documented in this inventory, so the penalty's use in practice remains unverified.

Whether non-Muslim residents of Borno are subject to the state statute's section 7 death penalty, or only to the federal SSMPA, is not addressed by the sources reproduced here; the UK Home Office note frames Islamic law as applying to Muslims.
